responses.reason: Before I accept a school nutrition slowdown for the $214,000 decline on account 4000 I would need revenue by customer segment for both months, the school accounts named and sized, and the prior July figure the sentence claims consistency with. I have seen none of it, because this table holds two months and no prior year column exists anywhere in the file. The seasonal story also sits awkwardly on June against July, since school accounts wind down as the academic year ends rather than a month later.

The pair is S7 and S8. S7 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year, and S8 says the $36,400 in July is the second phase of the dock program at Southline. I believe S8, because there is $36,400 of actual spend in account 6200 sitting under it and a booked cost beats a forward assertion every time. It matters to the close because a program with a second phase has a third, and S7 is the sentence that tells a reader there is no further commitment, which is exactly the representation that should not be wrong.

Account 7200 went $8,900 to $71,200, a $62,300 move at 700 percent, and it clears both limbs of the threshold with room to spare. Shrink is product that left the building without an invoice, so a sevenfold jump cannot be released on silence. I would ask which depots the loss sits in, whether it came from a physical count or an estimate, the count date and who supervised it, whether any of it is spoilage on refrigerated stock, and whether the same accounts were shrinking in smaller amounts in prior months.

The 1.9 is the percentage and the $1,900 is that percentage rewritten with a dollar sign. Account 7100 actually moved $76,300 less $74,900, which is $1,400, and $1,900 appears nowhere in the table. The sentence should read that interest expense rose $1,400, or 1.9 percent. I would also push on the driver, because a materially higher average revolver balance would move interest by more than 1.9 percent in a month, so either the draw was small or late in the month, and the daily balances would settle it.

The cost belongs in September, when the regional trade show takes place and the benefit is received. The entry should have been a debit to prepaid expenses and a credit to cash or accounts payable when the booth, space and deposits were paid, released to account 6600 in September as the show runs. As posted, July operating expense carries up to $96,400 that is not July's, which is most of the $74,400 movement. The sentence is circular on top of that, since saying July is elevated because July is elevated against a quiet June names no driver at all.

The driver belongs to account 5100, inbound freight, which fell $43,500 or 15.1 percent and is the only line a July 1 freight rate renegotiation could touch. The header keeps inbound freight separate from cost of product sold, so the two cannot borrow each other's explanations. What is left unexplained is the whole $147,000 on account 5000, and the likely answer is plain volume, since product revenue fell 3.8 percent while product cost fell 3.4 percent. That relationship is worth stating because cost fell slightly slower than revenue, so margin thinned rather than improved.

The conclusion does not survive, though the challenge has the figure wrong and I cannot reproduce $98,900 from anything in this table. Operating expense as the memo defines it, accounts 6000 through 7200, is $1,080,100 in June and $1,180,400 in July, against total revenue of $6,774,000 and $6,622,500. That is 15.9 percent and 17.8 percent, so it was never 15 percent in either month and the ratio deteriorated by about 188 basis points. Worse, the inference is backwards, because operating expense rose $100,300 or 9.3 percent while revenue fell $151,500 or 2.2 percent, so the cost base moved against volume and not with it.

Account 4200 moved $121,000 to $128,500, which is $7,500 at 6.2 percent, so it fails the $25,000 test and the 10 percent test and no driver is owed under the stated policy. The challenge also rests on a fact that is not in this file, since nothing here records a reclassification in this account last month and I have only June and July balances in front of me. Requiring a driver for $7,500 while account 7200 moves $62,300 with no sentence at all is effort aimed at the wrong line.

The amount does not exist. Account 4100 moved $1,041,000 to $1,096,000, which is $55,000 at 5.3 percent, and $38,000 is not a balance, a variance or a subtotal anywhere in this table. The premise fails as well, because a transfer needs an other side and no account here moved $38,000 in the opposite direction. The line is also below both threshold limbs so no commentary was required, and S2 attributing the growth to new maintenance contracts in Northgate and Tri-State is a perfectly ordinary explanation for a 5.3 percent move.

Account 6400 fell $62,000 to $9,500, which is $52,500 at 84.7 percent, so it clears both limbs of the threshold and is starred in the table, and a driver is genuinely owed. Silence is not acceptable here because the two possible causes point opposite ways. Either June carried a one-off specific reserve that simply did not repeat, which is benign, or part of the June provision was released back through income in July, which flatters the month by up to $52,500 and needs the receivable, the aging and what changed about collectability inside four weeks.

Account 6100 rose, it did not decline. $108,700 less $91,200 is an increase of $17,500, or 19.2 percent, and S4 tells the reader the opposite. That breaks the sentence in both halves, because the direction is wrong and diesel coming off its June peak would have pushed the line down. Fuel rising almost 20 percent in a month when product revenue fell 3.8 percent is the finding that should have been written, and it points at miles, routing or fleet condition rather than price.

Account 6000 went $702,500 to $781,900, which is $79,400, and S6 states $74,900. The difference is $4,500 and the digits are transposed, seven four nine against seven nine four. The table percent of 11.3 percent is computed off $79,400, so the memo disagrees with its own schedule on the largest expense in the company. The driver is wrong as well, since overtime for a summer volume peak cannot sit beside product revenue down $214,000 and product cost down $147,000 in the same month.

The fuel was burned in July so the cost belongs in July, and the entry should have been a debit to account 6100 and a credit to accrued liabilities for the estimated $9,800, reversed when the invoice posts in August. Calling that normal practice does not make it a policy, it makes it a standing cutoff failure that leaves the liability understated every month. The consequence is concrete, because $108,700 plus $9,800 is $118,500 against $91,200, an increase of $27,300 at 29.9 percent, which clears both threshold limbs and should have put fleet fuel on the starred list carrying commentary of its own.
